units.name: flask-app
units.role: The Flask application object: routing table, request dispatch, error handling, and WSGI serving.
units.description: This is the heart of Flask: the Application object a developer creates (Flask(__name__)) to build a web app. It holds the app's configuration, keeps the map of URL routes to view functions, decides which function should handle an incoming web request, runs 'before/after request' hooks, catches and reports errors, and turns whatever a view function returns into a proper HTTP response. It also knows how to talk to the outside world: it is itself a valid WSGI application a web server can call, it can start Flask's own development server, and it can hand out test clients so a developer's automated tests can pretend to be a browser talking to the app. It must never let one request's data leak into another's, and it must always run registered teardown/error handling even when a view raises.

units.name: scaffold
units.role: The shared registration vocabulary (route, errorhandler, before/after request, template filters) both App and Blueprint are built on.
units.description: This is the shared rulebook that defines what it means to 'register' something with a Flask application or a Blueprint: hooking up a URL route, declaring an error page, or running code before and after every request. Both the main application object and the Blueprint (a way to organize routes into reusable pieces) are built on top of this rulebook, so registering a handler works the same way and uses the same vocabulary whether it happens directly on the app or on a blueprint attached to it later. It also contains small helper logic for finding where a Python package lives on disk, used to locate an app's or blueprint's static/template folders.

units.name: blueprints
units.role: Groups routes/handlers/static+template folders into a reusable, named, nestable package that attaches onto an app.
units.description: This is Flask's blueprint system: the mechanism that lets a developer organize a set of routes, view functions, error handlers, and static/template folders into a reusable, named piece (a 'Blueprint') that can later be attached to a real web application, possibly nested inside other blueprints, and possibly attached more than once under different names or URL prefixes. It defers all setup work until the application actually registers the blueprint, at which point it merges the blueprint's routes and hooks into the application and, if configured, exposes the blueprint's own command-line commands and serves its static files. It must never apply its routes to an app until registration actually happens.

units.name: request-response
units.role: Flask's Request and Response wrapper classes, adding routing/blueprint/json awareness on top of Werkzeug's base classes.
units.description: This part of Flask defines the Request and Response objects that every view function receives and returns. They build on Werkzeug's basic web request/response building blocks but add Flask-specific conveniences: knowing which URL routing rule matched, what arguments were extracted from the URL, which blueprint handled the request, and configurable size limits (like maximum upload size) read from the app's configuration. These are the objects application developers interact with directly as `request` and when constructing responses to send back to a browser.

units.name: context
units.role: The push/pop lifecycle of 'what app and request are we currently handling', including teardown.
units.description: This is the part of Flask that keeps track of what application and request are currently being handled while code runs, and cleans up after itself when the work is done. When Flask starts handling a web request (or a CLI command), it creates a context object bundling the app, the incoming request, and the session, and pushes it so the rest of the code can find it. When the work finishes, the context is popped, which triggers registered cleanup (teardown) callbacks and fires push/pop notifications other parts of the app can listen for. It also provides a way to run a function after the current request finishes, a way to hand a background task a copy of the current request's context, and simple checks for whether a context is currently active. It must always run teardown even when the wrapped work raises an exception.

units.name: views
units.role: Class-based view pattern (View, MethodView) turned into ordinary dispatchable view functions.
units.description: This is Flask's class-based views feature. Normally a Flask page (a 'view') is just a plain function, but sometimes it is more convenient to write it as a class instead, for example to share setup code or to define one method per HTTP verb like GET/POST. This unit provides the base class View (and a specialization, MethodView, that automatically routes GET/POST/etc. requests to matching methods named get/post/... on the class) along with an as_view() helper that converts such a class into the ordinary callable function Flask's routing system expects.

units.name: helpers
units.role: Everyday functions view code calls: url_for, redirect, abort, flash, make_response, send_file, and small startup helpers.
units.description: This file provides the everyday convenience functions that Flask application developers call inside their view functions and templates: building URLs, redirecting users, returning error pages, showing one-time notification messages, shaping the final HTTP response, streaming a response while keeping request data available, and serving files or attachments to the browser. It also has a handful of small startup helpers that read configuration from environment variables and locate where an application's code lives on disk. These functions are the everyday toolbox application authors reach for, even though internally they mostly delegate to the active application object or the request/session context-locals.

units.description: This is Flask's collection of friendly, developer-facing error messages that only appear when an application is running in debug mode. Instead of a generic Python error, a developer who submits a file upload form without the right encoding, hits an unexpected routing redirect, or has a template that can't be found gets a clear explanation of what went wrong. Other parts of Flask reach into this toolbox on demand, only when debug mode is on, so these messages never slow down or clutter a production application.

units.name: context-locals
units.role: Contextvar-backed proxies (current_app, request, g, session, app_ctx) for finding 'the current app/request' from anywhere.
units.description: This file provides Flask's 'magic' global-looking variables: current_app, request, g, session, and app_ctx. Anywhere in a Flask application or extension, code can simply write `from flask import request` and get the request currently being handled, without it being passed down through every function call. Under the hood these are not real global variables but proxy objects that look up the currently active app/request via Python's contextvars, so each thread/task/greenlet sees its own current app and request. This file only defines the lookup mechanism and the proxy objects; it does not decide when a request or app 'becomes current' — that lifecycle is owned by the context unit.

units.name: config
units.role: Loads and stores app configuration from Python files, JSON/TOML files, objects, and environment variables.
units.description: This part of Flask manages an application's settings, such as whether debug mode is on or the secret key used to sign sessions. It provides a dictionary-like Config object that can be filled in several ways: pointing it at a Python file, a JSON/TOML file, an environment variable naming a file, a Python object/module, a plain mapping, or environment variables under a chosen prefix. It also provides ConfigAttribute, a small descriptor that lets other units expose individual config keys as normal-looking attributes (e.g. app.secret_key) that actually read and write through app.config underneath. It must never lose or silently coerce a setting a developer explicitly provided.

units.name: sessions
units.role: Signs, serializes, and verifies the session dict into and out of a browser cookie.
units.description: This part of Flask manages the user's session: a small dictionary of data a website wants to remember between one page visit and the next, like whether someone is logged in. Instead of storing this data on the server, Flask's default approach packs the dictionary into a tamper-proof, signed string and stores it in a browser cookie. This unit defines how to turn the session dictionary into a signed cookie value when sending a response, and how to read and verify that cookie value back into a dictionary when a new request comes in. It also defines a pluggable interface so a site could swap in a different storage mechanism while keeping the same session dictionary behavior. It must never accept a session cookie whose signature doesn't verify.

units.name: cli
units.role: The `flask` command-line tool: app discovery, .env loading, and the run/shell/routes commands.
units.description: This is the `flask` command a developer types in a terminal (and the `python -m flask` equivalent). units.description: This unit sets up Flask's built-in logging support. It provides the function that creates and configures each Flask application's logger, a helper that checks whether a logger already has a handler configured so Flask doesn't add duplicate output, and a stream object that points log messages to the correct output depending on whether a web request is currently being handled. Application authors can import these pieces directly to customize how their app logs errors.

units.name: signals
units.role: Blinker-based signal definitions other units send() and end users/extensions can subscribe to.
units.description: This unit defines Flask's named signals: announcements such as 'a request started', 'a request finished', 'an app context was pushed or popped', 'a template was rendered', or 'a message was flashed'. It doesn't decide when these things happen; other parts of Flask announce them here, and any code, inside Flask or written by an end user, can subscribe to be notified when they occur. It is a generic, content-free publish/subscribe bus; the lifecycle vocabulary lives in the units that send each signal.

units.name: testing
units.role: Simulates web requests and CLI invocations against a Flask app in-process, without a real server.
units.description: This code provides Flask's built-in testing toolkit: a way for developers to simulate web requests and command-line invocations against their app inside a test suite, without starting a real server or spawning a real process. It offers a test client that pretends to be a browser sending requests and getting back responses, a builder that assembles the fake request data using the app's own configuration, and a CLI runner that pretends to invoke the app's commands and captures their output. It also lets tests peek into and modify a user's session data during a simulated request.

units.description: This file defines the shared vocabulary of 'shapes' Flask uses to describe the different kinds of functions a developer can plug into their application, such as route handlers, error handlers, and before/after-request hooks. It contains no logic that runs while the app is serving requests; it exists so editors and type-checking tools can verify the right kind of function is being used in the right place. It has no behavior and no effects of its own, and is deliberately not treated as a dependency target for runtime calls elsewhere in this manifest, since nothing here is ever invoked, only imported for annotations.

violations_observed.location: src/flask/app.py (Flask methods reading self.view_functions, self.error_handler_spec, self.before_request_funcs, self.after_request_funcs, self.teardown_request_funcs, self.template_context_processors, self.url_value_preprocessors, self.url_default_functions)
violations_observed.note: Flask/App reach these as inherited instance state from Scaffold rather than through any narrow method Scaffold declares as an entrypoint; scaffold's contract only lists the Scaffold class itself, setupmethod, find_package, _endpoint_from_view_func, _sentinel, and jinja_loader. This is standard Python inheritance, not a bug, but it means the real boundary between 'scaffold' and 'flask-app' is wider than the declared entrypoints capture.

violations_observed.location: src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py (Blueprint.register merging self.deferred_functions and Scaffold-inherited registries onto the target app)
violations_observed.note: Same inheritance-based coupling as flask-app -> scaffold: Blueprint accesses Scaffold-inherited registries (view_functions, error_handler_spec, etc.) directly as shared instance state rather than through a declared entrypoint.
